tur49-0: Diabetic neuropathy is nerve damage caused by blood sugar that stays high over a long time; it most often causes burning, tingling and numbness in the feet. It affects up to half of people with diabetes. Although the damage cannot be reversed, its progression can be slowed. A daily foot check helps catch sores early, and balance and strength exercises help you walk more safely.

tur49-5: A 2025 review of 21 studies in older adults points the same way: for reducing fall risk, balance exercises and multicomponent exercise programmes helped most, followed by strength exercises.
tur49-6: Activities that are easy on your feet, such as walking, swimming, cycling, dancing and yoga, are also good options (NIDDK).
tur49-7: Yes, with a few precautions. In a review of eight trials (457 people), balance and strength exercises improved balance and fear of falling somewhat. Wear shoes that fit your feet well, check your feet after exercising and practise next to something you can hold on to. If you have an open sore on your foot, talk to your doctor first. The International Working Group on the Diabetic Foot (IWGDF) 2023 guideline also states that, for people at low or moderate risk of foot ulcers, an 8–12-week foot-ankle exercise programme, preferably supervised, can be considered, and that increasing daily steps by 1,000 is likely to be safe regarding ulcer risk; these are conditional recommendations based on low-certainty evidence.

tur49-11: Your blood levels need to be checked first. The American Academy of Sleep Medicine's 2024 guideline recommends that everyone with restless legs syndrome have their iron levels measured and that supplements be given according to these levels. Unnecessary iron can be harmful. According to the International Restless Legs Syndrome Study Group (IRLSSG) 2018 guideline, oral iron may be effective in people with a ferritin level of 75 µg/l or below (level of evidence: possibly effective); in moderate to severe symptoms, intravenous iron (ferric carboxymaltose) was found effective in people with ferritin below 300 µg/l. Your doctor decides which route is right for you.

tur49-15: Whether you need painkillers or anti-inflammatory medicines is your doctor's decision. Ice packs can ease the pain.
tur49-16: Most calcium deposits disappear on their own over time. Severe pain usually settles within a few weeks, but complete dissolving of the calcium can take up to 9 months, sometimes longer; milder pain may continue during this time.
tur49-17: The first step is pain control and keeping the arm as mobile as the pain allows. If the pain does not settle, your doctor may suggest a cortisone injection, ultrasound-guided breaking up and washing out of the calcium with a needle (lavage) or shockwave therapy. A review of three trials found that lavage may be more effective than shockwave therapy, and lavage combined with cortisone more effective than a cortisone injection alone; however, the quality of the evidence is low. Surgery is reserved for rare cases where pain cannot be controlled by other methods. In a randomised trial of 48 patients whose pain persisted despite other treatments, those who had a cortisone injection in addition to lavage improved more at 1 year than those who had a cortisone injection alone, and the risk of complications was low.
